newsitem.title: USA: Various CPI flavors pose dilemma for Fed -- SF Fed.
newsitem.headline: Various CPI flavors pose dilemma for Fed -- SF Fed.

text.p: The debate over whether the Consumer Price Index (CPI) overstates U.S. inflation is not the only one surrounding the popular price indicator.
Choosing which CPI to employ and how to use it properly as an efficient tool to forecast future inflation is seen as an even bigger dilemma for the Federal Reserve.

"The whole point of it is to try to figure out what represents permanent events and temporary events," said Brian Motley, a research official and economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco.
"If something purely temporary happens, which causes a rise in measured inflation but it's going to go away next month, then there is no real need for the Fed to do anything," Motley said.

"But if something is going on that implies inflation is going to be higher, not only this month but for several months or years in the future, then that might signal the need for the Fed to do something in the future," Motley told Reuters.
So how do you figure that out?
Motley said he has not discovered the Holy Grail of inflation forecasting formulas, but noted that some measures of price variations can be more efficient than others.
Motley argued that the median CPI may be the most accurate measure of inflation if one wants to look at a single indicator alone.

"If you want just one number to look at, to tell you what's going on, then it seems to me that the median may be a better number to focus on than the average because it's not going to be polluted by special events," Motley said.

Median price change is the level at which half of all price changes are larger and half are smaller. The method, the economist said, purges the sharpest price fluctuations in the inflation index and provides a cleaner inflation picture.
"This median technique .. essentially says we have to be agnostic about what causes price changes," he said.
Motley said the average CPI approach does not exclude sharp price fluctuations, as the median does, but incorporates them instead.

The San Francisco Fed economist said a simple exclusion of food and energy components in the so-called core rate of inflation also was far from perfect in terms of projecting the future behavior of prices.

"A general argument against a procedure that systematically excludes 'volatile' prices is that prices that move quickly may provide useful information about future trends that is not reflected in prices that change more slowly," the economist said.
Motley said the Fed currently examines a host of economic indicators and a variety of aspects of the consumer price index when setting monetary policy.

"The Fed, in practice, does not just look at one number. Given that you do not just look at one number, there is not much to choose between looking at the median, looking at the core, looking at overall CPI.
"But if you insist on looking at one number, then maybe the median is the number to look at," he said.
